early-home.q: What did Beauty’s mother hope he would never do, even in play?
early-home.evidence: I hope you will grow up gentle and good, and never learn bad ways; do your work with a good will, lift your feet up well when you trot, and never bite or kick even in play.”
early-home.hint: Look again at the mother’s advice.

early-home.q: Why did the bit feel so bad the first time?
options: It was a great piece of cold hard steel in his mouth
early-home.evidence: Those who have never had a bit in their mouths cannot think how bad it feels; a great piece of cold hard steel as thick as a man’s finger to be pushed into one’s mouth, between one’s teeth, and over one’s tongue
early-home.hint: Look again at the breaking in.

early-home.q: How did Beauty’s master get him used to the bit?
options: With oats, pats, kind words and gentle ways
early-home.evidence: and so, what with the nice oats, and what with my master’s pats, kind words, and gentle ways, I got to wear my bit and bridle.
early-home.hint: Look again at how the master treated him.

birtwick.evidence: “Yes,” she said, “he is really quite a beauty, and he has such a sweet, good-tempered face, and such a fine, intelligent eye—what do you say to calling him Black Beauty?”
birtwick.hint: Look again at the first ride.

birtwick.q: Why was the mare called Ginger?
options: She had a bad habit of biting and snapping
birtwick.evidence: “Ginger has a bad habit of biting and snapping; that is why they call her Ginger, and when she was in the loose box she used to snap very much.
birtwick.hint: Look again at what Merrylegs says.

birtwick.q: Ginger says nobody was ever kind to her when she was young. How might that explain her temper?
options: She learned to expect force, not kindness, from people
birtwick.evidence: “I never had anyone, horse or man, that was kind to me, or that I cared to please

storm.q: What fell right across the road in front of them?
options: An oak tree, torn up by the roots
storm.evidence: The words were scarcely out of his mouth when there was a groan, and a crack, and a splitting sound, and tearing, crashing down among the other trees came an oak, torn up by the roots, and it fell right across the road just before us.
storm.hint: Look again at the stormy road.

storm.q: Why did Sir Oliver have such a short tail?
options: It was cut off when he was young, for fashion
He lost it in a fight
storm.evidence: “For fashion!” said the old horse with a stamp of his foot
storm.hint: Look again at the talk in the orchard.

storm.q: Beauty would not step onto the bridge, even with the whip. What does the master say animals have?
options: A knowledge that can be quicker than human reason
storm.evidence: Master said, God had given men reason, by which they could find out things for themselves; but he had given animals knowledge which did not depend on reason, and which was much more prompt and perfect in its way, and by which they had often saved the lives of men.
storm.hint: Look again at what the master says afterwards.

fire.q: How did James get Beauty out of the smoky stable?
options: He tied his scarf over Beauty’s eyes and led him out
fire.evidence: It was on in no time; then he took the scarf off his neck, and tied it lightly over my eyes, and patting and coaxing he led me out of the stable.

fire.q: Why was the young man told to lay down his pipe?
options: He was going up into the hayloft
fire.evidence: “I say, Towler,” said the hostler, “just run up the ladder into the loft and put some hay down into this horse’s rack, will you? only lay down your pipe.”
fire.hint: Look again at the evening in the inn stable.

fire.q: James’s voice was “quiet and cheery” in the smoke. Why did that help?
options: A calm voice made the frightened horses trust him
fire.evidence: The next thing I heard was James’ voice, quiet and cheery, as it always was.
fire.hint: Think about how frightened the horses were.

night-gallop.q: How far did Beauty gallop to reach the town?
night-gallop.evidence: We came through a village, then through a dark wood, then uphill, then downhill, till after eight miles’ run we came to the town, through the streets and into the marketplace.
night-gallop.hint: Look again at the ride for the doctor.

night-gallop.q: Why did Beauty become ill after the gallop?
options: Joe did not put his warm cloth on him
night-gallop.evidence: He rubbed my legs and my chest, but he did not put my warm cloth on me; he thought I was so hot I should not like it.
night-gallop.hint: Look again at what Joe did in the stable.

night-gallop.q: John says Joe’s mistake was “only ignorance”. Why do people argue about that?
options: Not knowing can still cause great harm
John did not care about Beauty
night-gallop.evidence: “Only ignorance! only ignorance! how can you talk about only ignorance?
night-gallop.hint: Look again at the talk in the stable.

earlshall.q: Who was the new coachman at Earlshall?
earlshall.evidence: York, who was to be our new coachman, came in to see us.
earlshall.hint: Look again at the arrival at Earlshall.

earlshall.q: Why did the horses at Earlshall have to wear the bearing rein?
options: The lady wanted her carriage horses to look stylish
earlshall.evidence: I prefer a loose rein myself, and his lordship is always very reasonable about horses; but my lady—that’s another thing; she will have style, and if her carriage horses are not reined up tight she wouldn’t look at them.
earlshall.hint: Look again at what York says.

earlshall.q: Beauty began to dread having his harness put on. What had changed?
options: The bearing rein was made tighter day by day
earlshall.evidence: Day by day, hole by hole, our bearing reins were shortened, and instead of looking forward with pleasure to having my harness put on, as I used to do, I began to dread it.
earlshall.hint: Look again at how Beauty feels.

reuben.q: What was wrong with one of Beauty’s front shoes?
options: A nail had started to come loose
reuben.evidence: A nail in one of my front shoes had started as I came along, but the hostler did not notice it till just about four o’clock.
reuben.hint: Look again at the inn yard.

reuben.q: Why was Beauty sold from Earlshall?
options: His knees were marked and the earl would not keep them
reuben.evidence: The mare shall have a twelvemonth’s run, and we shall see what that will do for her; but the black one, he must be sold; ’tis a great pity, but I could not have knees like these in my stables.”
reuben.hint: Look again at what was decided.

reuben.q: The “steam-engine” drivers never got out to walk up a steep hill. What did they forget?
options: That a horse is a living creature who gets tired
reuben.evidence: They always seemed to think that a horse was something like a steam-engine, only smaller.

london.q: What did Jerry Barker’s family call his little daughter Dorothy?
london.evidence: The boy was twelve years old, a tall, frank, good-tempered lad; and little Dorothy (Dolly they called her) was her mother over again, at eight years old.
london.hint: Look again at Beauty’s new family.

london.q: Why wouldn’t Jerry drive fast for an extra shilling?
options: He wouldn’t overwork his horse to make up for other people’s lateness
london.evidence: “I will take you at the regular pace, gentlemen; shillings don’t pay for putting on the steam like that.”
london.hint: Look again at the late passengers.

london.q: Seedy Sam works fourteen or sixteen hours a day. What does his story show?
options: When drivers are treated harshly, their horses suffer too
london.evidence: I am on the stand fourteen or sixteen hours a day, and I haven’t had a Sunday these ten or twelve weeks
london.hint: Look again at what Sam tells the Governor.

hard-times.q: What did the doctor say Jerry must never go back to?
hard-times.evidence: Jerry grew better steadily, but the doctor said that he must never go back to the cab work again if he wished to be an old man.

hard-times.q: Why did the lady ask Jakes to take off the checkrein?
options: Beauty could not use all his power with his head held back
hard-times.evidence: he cannot use all his power with his head held back as it is with that checkrein
hard-times.hint: Look again at the steep hill.

hard-times.q: What helped Beauty recover after he fell?
options: Ten days of rest and good food
hard-times.evidence: Ten days of perfect rest, plenty of good oats, hay, bran mashes, with boiled linseed mixed in them, did more to get up my condition than anything else could have done

last-home.q: What did Farmer Thoroughgood say when he first saw Beauty?
options: “There’s a horse, Willie, that has known better days.”
last-home.evidence: “There’s a horse, Willie, that has known better days.”
last-home.hint: Look again at the horse fair.

last-home.q: Why did Willie want his grandpapa to buy Beauty?
options: He was sure Beauty would grow young in their meadows
Beauty was very cheap and fast
last-home.evidence: “But do look at his mouth, grandpapa, and ask the price; I am sure he would grow young in our meadows.”
last-home.hint: Look again at what Willie says.

last-home.q: Thoroughgood gives Beauty “in charge” to Willie. Why is that a good choice?
last-home.evidence: “you, Willie,” said he, “must take the oversight of him; I give him in charge to you.”
last-home.hint: Think about how Willie treats Beauty.

vault.q: How did the groom at Beauty’s last home know him?
options: By his white star, white foot and a patch of white hair
vault.evidence: “White star in the forehead, one white foot on the off side, this little knot just in that place;” then looking at the middle of my back—“and, as I am alive, there is that little patch of white hair that John used to call ‘Beauty’s threepenny bit’.
vault.hint: Think about the very last chapter.

vault.q: Who was the groom at Beauty’s last home?
vault.evidence: Beauty! do you know me?—little Joe Green, that almost killed you?”
vault.hint: Think about the very last chapter.

vault.q: What did Beauty’s ladies promise him?
options: That he would never be sold
vault.evidence: My ladies have promised that I shall never be sold, and so I have nothing to fear; and here my story ends.
vault.hint: Think about how the story ends.

vault.evidence: “Black Beauty—why, yes, I think that is a very good name.

vault.q: Why wouldn’t Beauty cross the wooden bridge in the storm?
options: It was broken in the middle
vault.evidence: “The bridge is broken in the middle, and part of it is carried away; if you come on you’ll be into the river.”

vault.q: What was the name of the cruel cab owner?
vault.evidence: His name was Nicholas Skinner, and I believe he was the man that poor Seedy Sam drove for.
